title: 3DG: A Framework for Using Generative AI for Handling Sparse Learner Performance Data From Intelligent Tutoring Systems
venue: LAK’24: International Workshop on Generative AI for Learning Analytics (GenAI-LA)
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of sparse learner performance data in intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs), where missing or limited quiz/attempt data can weaken learner modeling and knowledge tracing. The authors propose 3DG (3-Dimensional tensor for Densification and Generation), a framework that combines tensor factorization with generative AI to impute missing performance values and generate additional synthetic data samples.

The approach first represents learner interactions as a three-dimensional tensor over learners, questions, and attempts. Tensor completion is used to densify the sparse data, and then generative models are applied for augmentation. The paper compares GAN and GPT-4 for simulation of learning performance data, using clustering and power-law learning curves to tailor generation to different learning patterns. The empirical demonstration uses data from an AutoTutor reading comprehension lesson developed by the Center for the Study of Adult Literacy (CSAL), involving 118 adult participants in a U.S.-based ITS context.

The main conclusion is that tensor completion can effectively impute missing values in sparse ITS data, and that GAN produced more reliable simulations than GPT-4 for this numerical generation task. The authors argue that the framework may support more scalable and personalized educational modeling, while also noting that GPT-4 remains challenging to use for deep numerical simulation despite prompt engineering.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed methodological framework paper, not a causal evaluation of an educational intervention. It uses an existing AutoTutor dataset and compares generative simulation methods, but does not employ an experimental or quasi-experimental design to estimate learning impact.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper addresses a useful infrastructure problem for ITS research—handling sparse performance data—but it reports no direct student learning gains or educational effect sizes. Any impact is indirect and currently uncertain, so the practical impact on K-12 outcomes is unclear.

interventions.use_case: framework for imputing and augmenting sparse learner performance data from an AutoTutor intelligent tutoring system lesson using tensor completion plus generative models
data simulation framework applied to learner-question-attempt performance traces from a software-delivered reading comprehension lesson
